extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) working on U.S. patent prosecution
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for patent examination dealing with restriction/election of species (including Markush claims), transitional restriction procedures, nucleotide-sequence claim treatment, reissue restriction practice, and identification/handling of double patenting issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search continuation for Markush claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The search and examination of a Markush claim should be continued until either (1) prior art is found that anticipates or renders obvious a species that falls within the scope of a proper Markush grouping that includes the elected species, or (2) it is determined that no prior art rejection of any species that falls within the scope of a proper Markush grouping that includes the elected species can be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner need not extend the search beyond a proper Markush grouping. Continue examination of the Markush claim to determine whether it meets all other requirements of patentability (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 101 and 112, nonstatutory double patenting, and proper Markush grouping).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope limitation of Markush grouping search
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner need not extend the search to additional species that do not share a single structural similarity and a common use with the elected species (i.e., do not belong to the same recognized physical or chemical class or to the same art-recognized class and/or do not have a common use and/or do not share a substantial structural feature of a chemical compound and a use that flows from the substantial structural feature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search is confined to the proper Markush grouping; species outside that recognized group need not be searched.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of record on provisional election of species
rubrics_metrics.description: In the interest of compact prosecution, the examiner should ensure that the record is clear as to which species have been searched and have been found allowable over the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate if provisional election has been modified when additional species beyond elected species have been searched and determined allowable. Indicate withdrawal of provisional election if full scope of Markush grouping has been searched and determined allowable. Clarity of the record is critical to proper application of 35 U.S.C. 121 in later divisional applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction/maintenance only when serious burden exists
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner can only make or maintain any restriction requirement if there would be serious search and/or examination burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make/maintain restriction requirements absent a serious burden to search or examine the full scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on forcing scope narrowing for proper Markush claims
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may not seek to require an applicant to limit the scope of a claim that is directed to a proper Markush group to a subset of species that falls within the scope of the claim in the absence of a rejection of the claim for not complying with the requirements for patentability (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 101, 102, 103, and 112, and nonstatutory double patenting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes actions such as Ex parte Quayle or a Notice of Non-Responsive Amendment—cannot be used to force narrowing without a patentability rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of final rejection on provisional election
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim in a first application recites a proper Markush grouping encompassing patentably distinct inventions, and the claim is rejected over prior art in a proper final rejection, the examiner who required a provisional election need not continue to search the claim; the applicant's election loses its provisional status and is given full effect under 35 U.S.C. 121.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a divisional application is later filed claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 of the first application, the 35 U.S.C. 121 shield may be applicable so long as the consonance requirement is met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments canceling rejected species after final may be denied
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment canceling the rejected species received after final under 37 CFR 1.116 may typically be denied entry on the basis that it would require further consideration and/or search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such post-final amendments can be refused entry because they would change the scope and require further searching/examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition rights after final where election made with traverse
rubrics_metrics.description: If the applicant's provisional election was made with traverse and the requirement has been made final, the applicant may file a petition for review under 37 CFR 1.144.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §§ 818.01(c) and 818.01(d) for petition practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance preconditions for Markush claims
rubrics_metrics.description: No Markush claim can be allowed until any improper Markush grouping rejection has been overcome or withdrawn, and all other conditions of patentability have been satisfied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve improper grouping issues and ensure 35 U.S.C. 101, 112, nonstatutory DP, etc., are satisfied before allowance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional application eligibility under 37 CFR 1.129
rubrics_metrics.description: An application (other than reissue or design) pending for at least three years as of June 8, 1995, taking into account earlier applications under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, and 365(c), is subject to transitional procedures for limited examination after final rejection and restriction practice unless exceptions apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transitional provisions permit examination of more than one independent and distinct invention in the same application upon payment of fees, subject to the exceptions below.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to transitional restriction prohibition (37 CFR 1.129(b)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Restriction or divisional filing requirements may still be made/maintained if (i) the requirement was first made in the application or earlier relied-on application prior to April 8, 1995; (ii) the examiner has not made a requirement for restriction in the present or parent application prior to April 8, 1995 due to actions by the applicant; or (iii) the required fee for examination of each additional invention was not paid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only when one of these exceptions applies is a normal restriction requirement appropriate and telephone restriction practice may be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant options when restriction cannot be maintained (37 CFR 1.129(b)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: If restriction cannot be made or maintained under the transitional provision, applicant will be notified and given time to (i) elect invention(s) to be searched and examined and pay the fee for each extra invention; (ii) confirm a prior election and pay fees for additional inventions; or (iii) file a petition traversing the requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If petition filed timely, original time period for electing and paying is deferred and a new time period will be set; no petition fee is required under 1.129(b)(2). Unpaid inventions will be withdrawn under 1.142(b); applicant desiring examination can file a divisional under 35 U.S.C.121.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition/examples of 'actions by the applicant' preventing restriction prior to April 8, 1995
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions include (A) applicant abandoned and continued to refile so no Office action could issue, (B) applicant requested suspension of prosecution such that no Office action could be issued, (C) applicant disclosed multiple independent inventions but delayed presenting claims to more than one, and (D) applicant combined several applications into one continuing application but delayed filing so no restriction could be made prior to April 8, 1995.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In examples (A) and (B), a 3-month docketing prior to abandonment/suspension is prima facie evidence that applicant's actions did not prevent restriction. An extension under 37 CFR 1.136(a) does not constitute such actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referral to Technology Center Special Program Examiner for transitional exception issues
rubrics_metrics.description: If an examiner believes an application falls under the exception that no restriction could be made prior to April 8, 1995 due to applicant's action, the application must be brought to the attention of the Technology Center (TC) Special Program Examiner for review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use TC SPE review for borderline or discretionary determinations about the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph 8.41 for transitional restriction notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph 8.41 may be used to notify applicant that the application is a transitional application and is entitled to consideration of additional inventions upon payment of the required fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form paragraph should be used in all restriction or election of species requirements made in applications subject to 37 CFR 1.129(b). Procedure is NOT applicable to design or reissue applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refund when divided inventions rejoined due to linking claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever divided inventions in a transitional application are rejoined because a linking claim is allowable and applicant paid the fee for the additional invention, applicant should be notified that he or she may request a refund of the fee paid for that additional invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §§ 809, 821.04 and applicable transitional provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refund when additional species embraced by generic claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever claims drawn to an additional species in a transitional application for which applicant paid the fee are no longer withdrawn because they are fully embraced by an allowable generic claim, applicant should be notified that he or she may request a refund of the fee paid for that additional species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of when claims to a nonelected species would no longer be withdrawn should be made as indicated in MPEP § 806.04(d), § 821.04, and § 821.04(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of independence for nucleotide-sequence claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Polynucleotide molecules defined by their nucleic acid sequence that encode different proteins are structurally distinct and are thus deemed to normally constitute independent and distinct inventions within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. 121.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent evidence to the contrary, each such nucleotide sequence is presumed to represent an independent and distinct invention, subject to restriction per 35 U.S.C. 121 and 37 CFR 1.141 et seq.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical waiver/rescission for nucleotide-sequence claims
rubrics_metrics.description: In 1996 a partial waiver permitted a reasonable number of nucleotide sequences to be claimed in a single application; in 2007 the Commissioner rescinded that waiver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplemental restriction requirements will not be advanced in applications that already received an action on their merits for multiple nucleotide sequences except in extenuating circumstances; for national applications polynucleotide inventions follow MPEP Chapter 800 standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nucleotide sequences treated like other molecules for restriction/rejoinder
rubrics_metrics.description: For national applications under 35 U.S.C. 111(a), polynucleotide inventions will be considered for restriction, rejoinder, and examination practice in accordance with standards set forth in MPEP Chapter 800; claims considered for independence, relatedness, distinction and burden in same manner as claims to any other type of molecule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 1850 for PCT/national stage treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue restriction practice limited to original vs previously unclaimed subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Restriction between subject matter of the original patent claims and previously unclaimed subject matter may be required; restriction involving only subject matter of the original patent claims will not be required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If restriction is required, subject matter of original claims will be held constructively elected unless a disclaimer of all the patent claims is filed in the reissue application (which disclaimer cannot be withdrawn).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive election and withdrawal of new distinct reissue claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims of the original patent must not be restricted as being directed to two or more independent and distinct inventions and must be examined together. Any new claim directed to an invention that is independent and distinct from the invention(s) of the original patent claims will be withdrawn from consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may initiate a division of the claims by filing more than one reissue application in accordance with 37 CFR 1.177; see MPEP §§ 1450, 1451 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-recovery of non-elected inventions via reissue
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a restriction (including election of species) was made and applicant permitted the elected invention to issue as a patent without filing a divisional on the non-elected invention(s) or non-claimed distinct subject matter, the non-elected invention(s) and non-claimed distinct subject matter cannot be recovered by filing a reissue application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once applicant acquiesces to restriction and prosecutes elected claims to allowance, the only route is a timely-filed divisional; failure to timely file divisional is not error correctable by reissue. See MPEP § 1412.01 and cited case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of double patenting doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of double patenting seeks to prevent the unjustified extension of patent exclusivity beyond the term of a patent and to prevent prolongation of the patent term or multiple suits by different assignees on patentably indistinct variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public policy: upon expiration the public should be free to use the invention and obvious variants; double patenting occurs when another patent would unjustly extend exclusion rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commonality requirement for raising double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commonality of inventorship or (deemed) ownership must exist between two or more patents or applications before consideration can be given to an issue of double patenting (e.g., same inventive entity, at least one common joint inventor, common applicant/owner/assignee, or joint research agreement ownership).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 35 U.S.C. 100(f) and 100(g) definitions and MPEP §§ addressing prior art exceptions under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of double patenting rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: There are generally two types: (1) 'same invention' type double patenting rejection based on 35 U.S.C. 101, and (2) 'nonstatutory-type' double patenting rejection based on a judicially created doctrine intended to prevent prolongation of patent term by prohibiting claims in a second patent not patentably distinct from claims in a first patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The focus of DP analysis is on the claims in the multiple patents/applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer as response to nonstatutory double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: A terminal disclaimer, submitted per 37 CFR 1.321(c) or (d), includes a provision that the patent is enforceable only for and during such period that it is owned by the same party (or parties) that owns the other patents/applications identified in the terminal disclaimer that claim obvious variations of one invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminal disclaimer addresses equitable concerns about extending exclusivity; see In re Van Ornum and other cited authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstatutory double patenting includes anticipation/obviousness-based rejections and equitable extension concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonstatutory DP includes rejections based on anticipation, a one-way determination of 'obviousness', or a two-way determination of 'obviousness', and also includes rejections grounded in the equitable principle against permitting an unjustified timewise extension of patent rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'obviousness' analysis for 'obviousness-type' double-patenting is similar to, but not necessarily the same as, that under 35 U.S.C. 103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of charts and AIA/FTI distinctions in double patenting analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Charts are provided showing treatment of applications/patents having conflicting claims (same invention or patentably indistinct inventions), with FTI (first-to-invent) and AIA versions for use depending on the applicable 35 U.S.C. 102/103 regime of the involved applications/patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners may need to use FTI versions for earlier-filed applications subject to pre-AIA 102/103 and AIA versions for later-filed applications subject to post-AIA 102/103 (or vice versa). Charts show possible rejections if record supports them.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA chart guidance on 102(a)(2) provisional rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: AIA versions of the charts provide that a provisional rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) should not be applied if the earlier-filed application or patent is not prior art in view of 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(A) or (B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence necessary to show that a disclosure is inventor-originated (and thus excepted from being prior art) requires case-by-case analysis; if a prior inventor-originated public disclosure was outside the grace period, it may instead be prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1). See MPEP §§ 717 et seq. and 2155 et seq.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA chart limitations re transition cases and inventorship issues
rubrics_metrics.description: AIA versions of the charts do not address transition cases where pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(g) applies to applications subject to AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103, and do not address rejections under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 115 for improper naming of inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should consult MPEP § 2159.03 for transition applications and MPEP § 2157 for improper inventorship naming; consult Technology Center Practice Specialist as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances where double patenting issue can be raised
rubrics_metrics.description: A double patenting issue may arise between two or more pending applications, between one or more pending applications and a patent, or in reexamination proceedings between the patent claims being reexamined and claims of applications/patents. Double patenting does not relate to international applications not yet in national stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must determine whether grant of a second patent would give rise to an unjustified extension of rights granted in the first patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double patenting between issued patent and application
rubrics_metrics.description: Double patenting may exist between an issued patent and an application which share the same inventive entity, at least one common joint inventor, a common applicant, and/or a common owner/assignee, or where inventions result from activities under a joint research agreement as defined in 35 U.S.C. 102(c) or pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2) and (3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the inventor/applicant has secured a first patent, the examiner must determine whether a second patent would unjustifiably extend the rights in the first patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double patenting between copending applications and provisional rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may become aware of copending applications sharing common inventive entity/applicant/owner or joint research agreement issues that would raise double patenting problems if one became a patent; examiner may make a provisional double patenting rejection where doing so does not violate confidentiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Published unredacted applications can be used as double patenting references without violating confidentiality; unpublished or redacted applications can be used when they have at least one common joint inventor/applicant/assignee/owner or are deemed commonly owned. A provisional double patenting rejection should be made and maintained until obviated or no longer applicable.
